claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is governed by entropy-driven stabilization of a single-phase solid solution.
The initial high-entropy nanoalloy is a nominally homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
The nanoalloy will be subjected to extended high-temperature annealing.
Annealing will be performed above 0.6 times the alloy melting temperature and below the melting point.
An inert atmosphere will prevent oxidation during annealing.
The structural mediator is retention of a single-phase solid solution without phase separation or significant chemical ordering.
High configurational entropy reduces the free energy of the single-phase solid solution relative to phase-separated states.
High configurational entropy reduces the free energy of the single-phase solid solution relative to chemically ordered states.
The proposed configurational-entropy stabilization remains effective at elevated temperatures.
After high-temperature annealing, the nanoalloy will retain a single-phase solid solution without significant phase separation or chemical ordering.
A conventional binary or ternary alloy has lower configurational entropy than the high-entropy nanoalloy baseline.
A conventional binary or ternary alloy is expected to undergo phase separation or chemical ordering under the same annealing conditions.
The prediction is restricted to near-equimolar nanoalloys containing at least five principal elements.
Potential kinetic barriers to phase separation are not accounted for by the hypothesis.
Specific element combinations may influence nanoalloy stability independently of the proposed generic entropy mechanism.
XRD, TEM, and EDS can be used to compare phase constitution, microstructure, and elemental distribution before and after annealing.
Observation of significant phase separation or chemical ordering in the high-entropy nanoalloy under the specified conditions would falsify the hypothesis.
